[ORGANIZATION_A] initially started as a men's organization corresponding to [ORGANIZATION_A], but when it revised its charter in 1967, it opened membership eligibility to women as well, and as of 2004, the number of female ordinary members exceeded the number of male ordinary members. A person who agreed with the purposes of [ORGANIZATION_A] could become a member through the membership admission procedure. According to the charter and membership regulations of [ORGANIZATION_A], general members with voting rights and other rights were selected from among baptized and confirmed members of Christian churches who had paid a certain membership fee, had participated in [ORGANIZATION_A]'s activities continuously for at least two years as members, and were of a certain age or older, following recommendation by the Membership Committee and deliberation and decision by the Board of Directors. However, the membership department of [ORGANIZATION_A] had entirely excluded female members from the list of general members on the ground that [ORGANIZATION_A] had started as a men's organization and had been maintained and operated as a men's organization, and female members were in practice unable to become general members. In the case of male members, if they satisfied the general requirements described above and had no special grounds for disqualification, they were selected as general members. In response to the demands of female members, [ORGANIZATION_A] decided at its regular general meeting on February 22, 2003, to establish a Special Charter Revision Committee and a Special Reform Committee, and adopted a resolution stating that women and men would participate in the decision-making process on equal terms, that women would be granted the right to vote and the right to stand for election, and that gender-discriminatory factors would be eliminated. The Special Committee for Women proposed that practical steps be taken so that female members could become general members, and the Special Charter Revision Committee submitted a revision proposal to the Board of Directors. The Board of Directors of [ORGANIZATION_A] regarded women's participation in the general meeting as a matter for charter revision and decided that it would be determined by a resolution of the general meeting. It also decided that if more than half of the voters supported recognizing women's participation in the general meeting, the matter would be reflected in the regular general meeting the following year through the charter revision procedure. At the regular general meeting on February 26, 2005, the charter revision proposal was approved as originally proposed, but the votes in favor of recognizing women's participation in the general meeting did not reach more than half of the voters. [PERSON_GROUP_A] sent documents to [ORGANIZATION_A] in 2003, 2004, and 2006 requesting general-member authority or requesting that procedures be carried out to grant general-member status, but had not been selected as general members by those times. As members of [ORGANIZATION_A], [PERSON_GROUP_A] paid membership fees, but continuously lacked the opportunity to exercise voting rights at general meetings and other rights because they were women. Because the selection of [PERSON_GROUP_A] as general members was fundamentally restricted on the ground that they were women, [PERSON_GROUP_A] sent documents to [ORGANIZATION_A] in 2003, 2004, and 2006 requesting the granting of authority or a procedure for granting status. After not being selected as general members, [PERSON_GROUP_A] stopped paying membership fees after 2007. In this series of processes, [PERSON_GROUP_A] suffered mental harm. Around March 2004, 21 YMCAs in the Yeongnam and Honam regions recommended that [ORGANIZATION_A] grant female members general-member status. [ORGANIZATION_B] recommended on May 15, 2004, that general-member status be immediately granted to female members, and in June 2006 it resolved to implement withdrawal or equivalent sanctions if such status was not granted. In May 2004, [ORGANIZATION_C] confirmed that [ORGANIZATION_A] had excluded female members from voting rights at general meetings and other rights because they were women, and recommended that [ORGANIZATION_A] correct this. The National Assembly Gender Equality Forum, consisting of 83 lawmakers from governing and opposition parties, also expressed regret in May 2005 regarding [ORGANIZATION_A]'s discriminatory treatment and recommended prompt correction.

A bone marrow biopsy resulted in a diagnosis of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia (“AML”). Cytogenetic testing revealed significant chromosomal aberrations. On February 2, 2009, Walsh died.

source_evidence: For nearly forty years, Walsh served as a groundskeeper and golf course superintendent at several Pittsburgh area golf courses.
A bone marrow biopsy resulted in a diagnosis of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia (“AML”). Cytogenetic testing revealed significant chromosomal aberrations. On February 2, 2009, Walsh died.

Walsh’s executor commenced this wrongful death and survival action against the manufacturers of various pesticides that he had applied during his career, asserting claims in strict products liability, negligence, and breach of warranty.

new_text: [COMPANY_B] was a professional consulting engineering firm, [PERSON_B] was its president, and [PERSON_A] had worked for [COMPANY_B] as a professional land surveyor for many years and headed its survey department during the relevant events. In 2006, [PERSON_A] regularly accepted surveying work independent of his work for [COMPANY_B] with [PERSON_B]’s permission, used his own equipment for that work, and performed it outside his 40-hour workweek for [COMPANY_B]. [COMPANY_B] did not bill clients for work [PERSON_A] performed independently, which included elevation surveys. [PERSON_C] was one of the owners of [COMPANY_A], a company that sold medical equipment for use by elderly people and people with disabilities. Around September 2006, [PERSON_C] contacted [COMPANY_B] about surveying a property [COMPANY_A] had purchased in [LOCATION_A]. [COMPANY_B] sent [PERSON_A] to speak with [PERSON_C] about that property. After [PERSON_A] began work there, [PERSON_C] asked him to perform an elevation survey and complete an elevation certificate for property in [LOCATION_B]. [PERSON_A] made two trips to the [LOCATION_B] property and worked approximately 10 to 15 hours on the survey. He used his own surveying equipment and did not drive a company vehicle. On the elevation certificate, he listed his title as “Land Surveyor,” left “Company Name” blank, and listed his home address. He gave [PERSON_C] a handwritten invoice that listed his personal address and did not refer to [COMPANY_B]. [COMPANY_B] did not issue an invoice for [PERSON_A]’s work at the [LOCATION_B] property and was not paid for that project. Twenty days after [PERSON_A] completed the elevation certificate, [PERSON_C] signed a check dated November 1, 2006, from [COMPANY_C] payable to [PERSON_A] for [CURRENCY_AMOUNT_A]. After completing the work, [PERSON_A] realized that he had made a 30.48-meter error on the flood-elevation certificate: he recorded a base flood elevation of approximately 180.75 meters instead of approximately 211.84 meters for Buildings 1 through 5. [PERSON_C] alleges that this error caused the certificates to incorrectly state that the [LOCATION_B] property was outside the 100-year flood plain. [PERSON_B] testified that [PERSON_A] was acting independently when he worked on the [LOCATION_B] property, that the work was not a project of [COMPANY_B], that [COMPANY_B] was not paid for it, that [COMPANY_B] did not send [PERSON_C] or [COMPANY_A] an invoice for it, and that [PERSON_B] did not know about the work until months later, when [PERSON_A] spoke with him about the error.

new_text: In December 1999, [PERSON_A] suffered a fatal accident while driving an off-highway dump truck within the scope of his employment with [COMPANY_A], the general contractor on a construction site owned by [ORGANIZATION_A]. On the afternoon of December 1, 1999, [COMPANY_A] asked [PERSON_A], who usually drove water trucks on the site, to drive a loaded, heavy-duty, off-highway dump truck up a hill on a haul road, even though he had never driven that type of truck on this worksite. Testimony indicated that [PERSON_A] was apprehensive about driving that type of truck but accepted the assignment. [COMPANY_A] constructed temporary unpaved haul roads to transport materials between sections of the project. Testimony indicated that [COMPANY_B] inspectors had authority to act regarding safety violations on haul roads and could stop work if they perceived a dangerous condition. [COMPANY_A] had no contractual relationship with [COMPANY_B], and its contract with [ORGANIZATION_A] assigned [COMPANY_A] responsibility for the safety of its employees on site. [COMPANY_B] contended that [PERSON_A] drove off the road to avoid an oncoming grader despite having sufficient room to pass. [PERSON_B] asserted that the haul road collapsed because instability in the hill caused by coal seams. [PERSON_B] alleged that the haul road should have had flaggers, barricades, or radio contact for truck drivers. She also alleged that [COMPANY_B] failed to require proper construction and maintenance of the haul road and failed to inspect it. [COMPANY_B]'s safety monitor was to represent [ORGANIZATION_A] in construction-safety matters, review and approve contractor emergency procedures and site-safety plans, interview applicants for contractors' safety representatives, monitor those representatives' performance, and monitor contractors' compliance with applicable safety regulations at all work operations on a frequent and regular schedule. [PERSON_A] suffered fatal injuries when the truck plunged down an 8.5-meter embankment and landed upside down in 1.2 meters of water. [COMPANY_B] asserted that [PERSON_A]'s death resulted from the construction and maintenance of the haul road by [COMPANY_A]. An expert stated that [COMPANY_B]'s representative traveled on haul roads but did not notice steep grades, narrow width, faulty slope configuration, inadequate drainage, or the absence of a safety berm, and did not address hazardous weather conditions on the day of the accident despite concerns expressed by employees.

Plaintiff specifically alleged that the haul road should have been equipped with various safety features such as flaggers to direct traffic, barricades, or radio contact for the truck drivers.

source_evidence: On May 9, 2012, nine-year-old Jarrett Brewington participated in a relay race during gym class at Walter G. Smith Elementary School, in Philadelphia.
No padding covered the gym wall, which was made of concrete.

Mother alleged that Jarrett’s injuries occurred because of a defective and dangerous condition of the premises — namely, the concrete gym wall — and that the School was negligent in failing to install padded safety mats to cushion the wall.
Jarrett himself testified that his injury occurred because he was running too fast and tripped and fell.

[ORGANIZATION_B] alleged that the wall had no defect or condition that caused [PERSON_A]’s injury and that the injury instead resulted from a teacher directing students to run toward the wall and from [PERSON_A] tripping and falling. [PERSON_A] testified that he was injured because he was running too fast, tripped, and fell.

[ORGANIZATION_C]는 2004년 5월 [ORGANIZATION_A]가 여성이라는 이유로 여성회원들의 총회의결권 등을 배제한 사실을 확인하고 [ORGANIZATION_A]에 시정을 권고하였다. 여야 국회의원 83명으로 구성된 국회양성포럼도 2005년 5월 [ORGANIZATION_A]의 차별적 처우에 대해 유감을 표명하고 신속한 시정을 권고하였다.
